feedback: Safe choice: 'You're inside and safe — now you can watch the storm from indoors, a little way back from the window.'
Tree choice: 'A tall tree is one of the riskiest places in a storm because lightning tends to hit the tallest thing — let's get inside instead.'
Water/open-ground choice: 'Open ground and water aren't safe in a storm — head for a building or a car.'
Keep every corrective message calm and empowering, never frightening.
activities.intendedInsight: Staying safe in a storm is a decision you can make and rehearse: go indoors or into a car, and the right action becomes familiar so you feel in control rather than frightened.
learnerActions: Watch or imagine a storm rolling in — dark clouds gather and a rumble of thunder sounds.
Choose where to go: a house, a car, under a big tree, an open field, or beside a swimming pool.
When you choose a safe place (house or car), see yourself safe and cosy indoors, watching the storm from a little way back from the window.
When you choose an unsafe place, read the kind, un-scary prompt explaining why it is risky (e.g. 'a tall tree is one of the riskiest places — let's get inside instead') and try again.
Repeat the 'hear thunder → go inside' decision several times until it feels familiar.
activities.title: Storm scenario: choose where to go

feedback: Correct sort: confirm the rule and its reason, e.g. 'Right — a building protects you because if lightning hits it, the building carries the lightning around you and down into the ground.'
Tree placed as safe: 'A tree shelters you from rain but NOT from lightning — it's actually one of the least safe places.'
activities.intendedInsight: A tree is for rain shelter, not storm safety; the safe places are indoors or a car, and open or wet places are dangerous.
learnerActions: Sort places and things into 'safe in a storm' and 'not safe in a storm'.
Safe: inside a building, inside a hard-topped car.
Unsafe: under a tall tree, in an open field, in or beside a swimming pool, pond or the sea.
For each one, say the reason aloud — e.g. 'a tall tree is unsafe because lightning tends to hit tall things'.
activities.title: Safe place / unsafe place sort

feedback: 'Thunder is just a loud noise — it can't hurt you, but it tells you lightning is near. The danger is lightning, and being inside keeps you safe.'
'Storms are natural. There are safe places to go — buildings and hard-topped cars — so you can act and stay safe.'
If a conversational persona is used, keep it strictly bounded to correct, calm storm-safety guidance.
activities.intendedInsight: Storms can feel scary because they are loud, but thunder is only the sound; following simple rules helps keep you safe, so you can feel in control.
learnerActions: Look at a scene of a child safe indoors, watching a storm from inside.
Hear or read the message that thunder is just a loud sound — it can't hurt you, but hearing it means lightning is near; the thing to stay away from is lightning, and being indoors protects you.
Talk about how storms are natural events, not something out to get you, and that knowing what to do helps you feel safe.
Optionally ask a caring, reassuring character a worry such as 'is thunder going to hurt me?' and talk through what to do.
activities.title: Calm reassurance: thunder is just a sound

feedback: Correct: confirm and extend — 'Yes, go indoors or to a car, and stay away from tall trees and water.'

Partial (knows to go in but not why): add the reason — 'Lightning tends to hit tall things out in the open, and a building or hard-topped car carries the lightning around you into the ground, so inside you're protected.'
activities.intendedInsight: You can state at least two thunderstorm safety rules and say why indoors is safest.
learnerActions: Answer: 'What should you do when you hear thunder?' — choosing 'go inside a building or car' over unsafe options.
Explain in your own words why indoors is safer than being out in the open.
Name one more thing to stay away from (tall trees, open ground, or water).
activities.title: What should you do? quick check
